TO THE 
CONFERENCE? 


EDITORIAL 


by C. F. Plewman 


On March first and second, we will 
see the tenth annual Camping Confer¬ 
ence, this year at the Royal York Hotel 
in Toronto. 

With camp people this raises the 
question — why go to the conference? 
Has it anything to teach us? Won’t it 
be like all of the previous ones? Has it 
anything new or different to offer? 

The answer to these questioas is to he 
found in ourselves as much as in the 
nature of the conference. 

Granted that we are keen about 
camping, that we want to make our 
camp a better one, that we want to learn 
more about helping youngsters to hit it 
off on all eight cylinders; I say granted 
this, it is difficult to understand how one 
could participate in such a gathering 
without being helped. Just as the highly 
trained physician who has completed a 
lengthy academic course finds it neces¬ 
sary to attend conventions where the 
latest findings and discoveries in the 
field of medicine are discussed, so like¬ 
wise, we in camping have to keep our¬ 
selves abreast of new developments and 
better techniques if we are to make our 
greatest contribution. 

It is a fatal mistake to think that we 
in camping are not affected by our ever- 
changing, rapidly devolping civilization. 
I can remember the time when girls’ 
camps were practically unheard of, 
when boys under age thirteen were not 
allowed to attend camp, when night air 


Toronto , Canada , February , 1957 


had been thought to be unhealthy; in a 
a word, a time when only the more 
venturesome of parents would even con¬ 
sider sending their boy to a camp. As 
for a girl, why, that was just out of the 
question. There can he no doubt that 
times change. The $64,000 question is: 
Are we changing with it? 

A conference means many things to 
many people. In any case, a conference 
is something more than listening to 
speeches. It is also discussing conflicting 
viewpoints. A conference is something 
more than discussion groups, it is also a 
marvellous time for happy fellowship. A 
conference is something more than just 
plain “getting”. It is also a place for 
“giving”. 

I am convinced that some people 
benefit far more from conferences than 
do others. Nor is the answer hard to 
find. For one thing, their presence there 
is no accident; rather is it the result of 
deliberate planning. They know why 
they are there and what it is they are 
after. Their conference activities are 
highly selective. It is anything but a 
case of hit and miss. Ask them why they 
are there and they will tell you—to meet 
friends, have fun, discuss problems, 
compare notes or to pick up new ideas, 
check on old ones, look at the exhibits, 
view the literature, to rub shoulders and 
last but not least, to feel and to know 
that they are, in very truth, an integral 
part of this intangible yet wonderful 
thing we call The Camp Movement. 

continued on page 57 


If) 




DO WE PUT FIRST THINGS FIRST? 


The Rev. Wilbur K. Howard 

Associate Editor, Sunday School Publications, United Church of Canada 


A successful camp depends upon the 
discovery of what is first in camping 
and then upon putting it first. This 
sounds trite but it’s right. A little more 
difficult is how to determine just what 
does come first in camping. 

There are some confusing contrasts 
in the field of camping. Some say that 
camp should offer the camper adven¬ 
ture, spiced with the sting of danger 
and the thrill of risk. Others say that 
camp should offer security. Some point 
to camp as an opportunity to get out of 
doors. Others, meanwhile, are building 
deluxe dining halls and comfortable 
cabins. Some belong to the rough-it- 
school, the let-the-rain-beat-in-your- 
face school. Others press hard for 
greater safety, better sanitation—keep 
your feet dry. Some tell us that camp 
is important because it is a complete 
change from school. Others are equally 
vocal in asserting that camp is the most 
significant twentieth century educa¬ 
tional technique. Some contend that 
camp should off er campers a permissive 
atmosphere—freedom from supervision. 
Others are busy defining the respon¬ 
sibilities of Camp Directors, program 
directors, sectional directors, unit direc¬ 
tors, counsellors, assistant counsellors, 


counsellors in training, campers in 
training for counsellors in training. 
Some have maintained that camping is 
simple living in the outdoors. Others 
have avowed that camping is the 
adjustment of the individual in a highly 
complex community which involves the 
adaptive social function of anxiety, the 
professional services of such experts as 
psychologists, psychiatrists, group work¬ 
ers, case workers, dietitians, doctors, 
nurses, and counsellors who can fill in 
form 249D8. There are those who tell 
us that camping means getting away 
from the city. On the other hand, 
there are those who say: “Straighten 
those trails!” “Prune those trees!” “Let’s 
go into town for a spree!” Some main¬ 
tain that camp should present to the 
camper the joys of rest, sleep and leis¬ 
urely living. Others are firm in the 
belief that camp should give the camper 
hills to climb, stiff swimming tests, 
back-breaking portages, trails that are 
crooked, callouses on the palms. And 
then there are those who hold out that 
camp should take the camper away 
from the strains and stresses of civiliza¬ 
tion only to be completely frustrated by 
those who contend that camping must 
save the world. 


16 


Canadian Camping 




However, in spite of confusing con¬ 
trast and conflicting opinions, there is 
one important common factor in the 
field of camping—human personality. 
The end product in camping is not a 
tin of tomato soup, a plastic bowl or a 
frigidaire. It is human personality. It 
would seem reasonable to suggest, then, 
that what we put first in camping is 
the highest development of human 
personality. 

Putting the highest development of 
human personality first puts camping in 
line with the greatest purposes and 
ultimate achievements of mankind. It 
gives camping a purpose that money 
can’t buy or rules can’t force. It gives 
camping a purpose that is bigger than 
camping itself. 

What does putting the highest devel¬ 
opment of human personality first mean 
for the camp owner? It means that the 
camp owner, like the school teacher, the 
social worker or the minister, must be 
motivated by a desire to render unselfish 
service through helping his fellow man. 

What does putting the highest devel¬ 
opment of human personality first mean 
for camp leadership? It means that in 
approaching a potential camp leader 
your primary concern will not be, has 
he had any camping experience, but 
rather, how does he stack up in the 
business of living?—has he got the abili¬ 
ty to influence significantly the attitudes 
and behaviour of other persons? It will 
mean not only a careful examination of 
written references but a knowledge of 
the ability of the persons who gave the 
references. It will mean the follow-up 
of written references with personal 
conversation. It is surprising the things 
that people know that they would never 
think of writing down. It will mean 
securing references that will tell you 
something about the total personality of 
the potential leader, not just one or two 
outstanding things in which he excels. 


Being concerned first about the high¬ 
est development of human personality 
will mean a new status for the counsel¬ 
lor. It is in the small tent or cabin 
groups that campers are most influ¬ 
enced. The counsellor in his field must 
be just as much an expert as the riding 
instructor, the swimming instructor or 
the camp nurse. The counsellor must 
understand the campers with whom he 
works. He must have a genuine liking 
for his campers. This will be indicated 
not only in the way he acts when he is 
with his campers, but also the way he 
talks about his campers when he lets 
down his hair in front of his fellow 
counsellors. The counsellor must have 
the necessary know-how regarding the 
philosophy of camping, group work, 
the techniques of leadership. If the 
counsellor is expected to keep neat and 
accurate records, he must be given 
adequate facilities to do so efficiently. 
Help in regard to records is indicated 
if the records take so much time that 
the counsellor is forced to be away from 
his cabin group when the group needs 
him. This paper curtain between coun¬ 
sellor and cabin group must be done 
away with. It may mean introducing 
better and quicker ways of doing records 
such as the use of dictaphones, wire 
recorders, stenographic help. 

What does this primary concern for 
the highest development of human per¬ 
sonality mean for the camper? It means 
that the campers have a real share in 
the running of the camp. Wilbur C. 
Hallenbeck, of Teachers College, Col¬ 
umbia University, has said: “One of 
the things most devastating to human 
personality is that characteristic of our 
modern world which has deprived indi¬ 
viduals of their right to have something 
to say about what happens to them.” 
Houseman said the same thing in an¬ 
other way— 

“I am alone and afraid 
In a world I never made.” 

continued on page 38 


Toronto , Canada , February , 1957 


17 


I’m just an average director, running 
the average camp. Our camp is no 
more elaborate than most and doesn’t 
require any more insurance coverage 
than most camps—whether organiza¬ 
tional or private. Therefore, what I 
have to say in this artcle, pertains to 
YOU, so pay heed! 

Most of us, when wondering or asked 
about a certain insurance coverage, feel 
certain that we are protected. Feeling 
fairly certain is not good enough. You 
must be absolutely positive. Don’t find 
this out the hard way (as some directors 
have)—when you have a claim. Then it 
is too late. Now is the time to carefully 
go over your policies to make sure. I 
might suggest that you have your poli¬ 
cies with you as you peruse this article 
and check them as you go along. 


should have a fire loss of $50,000, it 
doesn’t mean that you will collect that 
amount regardless of what. Do you 
know that you must carry insurance for 
at least 90% of the total value of your 
holdings to collect the full amount of 
your loss ? Another reason for reviewing 
with regard to increasing your insured 
amounts. 

Do the policies covering contents of 
the camp in case of fire, cover the 
belongings of campers and staff, if a fire 
should occur during the season? 

If you transfer office furniture, sup¬ 
plies, typewriters, etc. to the city for the 
winter, do you have a policy to cover 
them? Because they have to do with a 
business, it is doubtful your household 
fire policy would cover them. 


ARE you ADEQUATELY INSURED? 


FIRE. We’ll start with fire insurance, 
as we all carry that. No doubt your fire 
insurance was placed many years ago. 
Have you taken the time to review the 
amounts for which you are insured? 
Have you increased them? If not, you 
should have! You are well aware that 
values have increased greatly in the past 
few years. Could you replace your 
buildings and their contents for the 
amounts you are now insured for if you 
were to have a fire to-day? If you 
haven’t reviewed your fire insurance 
within the past four years, you had 
better do it now! 

What about the co-insurance clauses 
on your policies? Do you thoroughly 
understand what they mean? If you 
have $50,000 worth of fire insurance 
with a 90% co-insurance clause and you 


BUSINESS INTERRUPTION. This 
is one coverage that many of us don’t 
carry. It protects you against loss of 
revenue, if you were to have a fire near 
or during the season, which would pre¬ 
vent you from operating or operating 
on a reduced scale and be unable to 
obtain the revenue you would have, if 
the fire hadn’t occurred. Remember, a 
fire shortly before or during the sum¬ 
mer, could wipe out your earnings for 
an entire year. 

GENERAL LIABILITY. This is 
probably your most important coverage. 
It is the policy that protects you in the 
event of claims, legal suits, etc., if a 
camper, visitor or even an off-duty staff 
member should be injured, taken ill or 
lose his life, from any cause which could 
be blamed on your negligence whether 


18 


Canadian Camping 









it was carelessness or not. If your camp 
has boats of any description, riflle range, 
horses, tuck shop, the insurance company 
must be aware of all details concerning 
these. Make sure your policy reads to 
cover campers while going to and from 
camp or away on trips, if they are under 
the supervision of your staff. 

What about the limits of your liability 
policy? Are they high enough? It costs 
very little more to increase these limits. 
The amount to increase your protection 
from $50,000 for death or injury to one 
person and $100,000 for death or injury 
to two or more persons, to $100,000 and 
$200,000, is negligible. To-day, with 
everyone being so “claims conscious”, 
legal suits for damages for fantastic 
amounts, are very common. 


icy passenger hazard coverage does not 
cover in the above eventuality. 

Our experience with this was odd. 
We had our general liability written 
with one company and our automobile 
insurance with another. Both companies 
insisted it was the responsibility of the 
other company to cover it. The only 
way we settled the problem, was to 
place both the liability and auto insur¬ 
ance in the same company. My advice 
is that you have your camp vehicles 
covered (if you carry campers in the 
back of your truck, make sure the 
insurance company is aware of this) for 
this special passenger hazard coverage 
and that campers are carried in no 
other vehicles. 


ARE you POSITIVE? 


by W. Bertram Danson, 
Director, Camp Winnebagoe 


Another thing to remember about 
liability, is that this policy does not 
cover for death or injury to a camper 
who may be riding in you car, the camp 
truck or a staff member’s car, while 
going on a trip, in town to the doctor 
or anywhere. You can have your policy 
endorsed to give you coverage for this, 
but you will have to pay an extra 
premium for each vehicle so covered. 
In Ontario, we have a law that says a 
car owner isn’t liable for death or injury 
to anyone in his car in the event of an 
accident. Of course taxis, buses or any 
others receiving compensation for carry¬ 
ing the person are excluded from this 
law. If you are receiving a fee to keep 
the child at camp, the responsibility is 
yours until the child is returned to the 
hands of his parents. Therefore, you too 
would be liable. The ordinary auto pol- 


Tor onto, Canada , February, 1957 


AUTOMOBILE. Of course we all 
carry the usual public liability, property 
damage, fire and theft insurances on our 
cars. Again, are our limits on these high 
enough? Remember, the cost of in¬ 
creased limits is very low. 

Don’t forget to cancel all insurance, 
other than fire and theft on vehicles that 
you “lay-up” for the winter. You can 
save yourself quite a few dollars by 
doing so. Are your vehicles which are 
used excusively at and in the district 
around camp, insured as of that terri¬ 
tory? The rates are much lower in the 
country than in the city. 

NON-OWNED AUTO. If anyone is 
on camp business—calling on campers, 

continued on next page 


19 







doing messages in town, going to the 
railway station, etc., with his own car 
and becomes involved in an accident, 
the camp can be held partially respon¬ 
sible, whether or not the car owner has 
insurance of his own. Non-owned auto 
insurance will protect your interest from 
claims of the party with whom your 
staff member had the accident. The 
cost here is low and worth having. 

If your campers are transported any¬ 
where on buses and there was an acci¬ 
dent, you could be held jointly liable 
with the bus company. A non-owned 
auto policy would protect you. 

HOLD-UP. Inside and outside. Re¬ 
imbursement for loss of funds taken 
from you by threat of violence, while in 
your city or camp office, going to the 
bank or travelling anywhere with camp 
money. Cost is low. 

BURGLARY. This covers for loss of 
your equipment, belongings, etc. if any 
building is broken into, either during or 
off season. However, please remember, 
that there must be evidence of a forced 
entry. 

SAFE BURGLARY. An inexpensive, 
but fireproof safe is advisable for all 
camps, to keep money, the camp books 
and valuables left with the camp by 
campers for safe keeping. Safe burglary 
covers in the event of a loss, should the 
safe be broken into. 

CAMERA FLOATER. Most camp 
directors have cameras, projectors, etc. 
A camera floater will protect them for 
loss by fire, theft and even breakage, 
whether in your home, car, at camp or 
anywhere. 

MOTOR BOAT. Protection for your 
outboard motors and boats. Covers if 
motor is stolen, takes fire or is lost over¬ 
board. Your boats are covered too— 
even while in transit on your trailer! 


BOILER. If you have any hot water 
heating system, larger than a jacket 
heater, it should be insured as a “pres¬ 
sure object”. Consult your insurance 
company and give them a description of 
the equipment. They will advise you. 

WORKMEN’S COMPENSATION. 
For some years now, Children’s Camps 
have come under the Workmen’s Com¬ 
pensation Act. This means that it is 
compulsory for all camps to be covered 
by Workmen’s Compensation. Any 
camp not so covered, is liable for assess¬ 
ment of back fees for the years they 
weren’t covered (and should have been) 
plus interest, if the Board should discov¬ 
er they weren’t complying with the Act. 
However, our experience has been that 
the Board is very understanding. So, if 
you haven’t had your camp covered 
previously, you had better contact it 
right pronto! 

Of course, this eliminates the necessity 
for the old Employers Liability policy 
we previously carried. We now get a 
much broader coverage for less money. 
And the beauty of it is, it can’t be 
cancelled. 

Mr. Director: you can be included 
on your Workmen’s Compensation cov¬ 
erage, if you desire. My recommendation 
is that you do so. Since much of your 
time is spent on camp business of one 
kind or another, it is an advantage to 
have this additional protection for 
yourself at little extra cost. 

CAMPER’S HEALTH AND ACCI¬ 
DENT INSURANCE. This is one of 
the newer coverages available to camps. 
Many of us have had it for the past tour 
or five years and each year more camps 
take advantage of it. It can be secured 
to cover all of your campers or only 
some. Some camps include this coverage 
for their campers in their fee. Others 
have it as an optional plan, if the

Canoeing . . . 

c4 Canadian .Heritage 

*' ■’ A -• ■’ u .. 

p ART i _ IT’S ROMANTIC ORIGIN 


Canoeing is an integral part of 
Canadian history and tradition. The 
canoe itself has been claimed as the 
most important factor responsible for 
the exploration, settlement and develop¬ 
ment of this country. Not only was it 
. the principal means of transportation 
; for . the native Indians but also for the 
explorer, voyageur, fur trader, mission¬ 
ary and settler. . 

The origin of the canoe is shrouded 
in mystery, speculation and sentiment. 
Stories about the canoe are frequent in 
Indian folklore. Perhaps the most 
familiar legendary canoeist is Hiawatha, 
described in Longfellow’s poem; In 
some myths, life after death is described 
as floating down a river in a strange 
canoe. The stone canoe occurs in leg¬ 
ends of many tribes, from the Micmacs 
of Nova Scotia to the Chippewas of the 
North West Territories. 

French Canadians still tell their child¬ 
ren the story of the Legendary “Chasse 
Galerie” or flying canoe. To the early 
settlers, the birch-bark canoe seemed to 
fly over the water like a magic bird, but 
the folk tale tells of a flying canoe which 
was paddled through the air by home¬ 
sick lumbermen who wished to see their 
families at New Year’s. The Devil was 
supposed to offer this reprieve. The men 
could paddle over mountains and roof¬ 
tops if they wore no sacred emblem, hit 
no steeples and returned before mid¬ 
night. 


by Mary Porter 

This is the first of a series of three articles 
on Canadian Canoeing written by Miss Mary 
Porter for Canadian Camping* We present 
them in the hope that counsellors and direct¬ 
ors will use them to read to campers so that 
they, in turn, will know something of our 
Canadian heritage. 


The name canoe is of controversial 
origin. It is probably derived from the 
French word ‘canot’, which means hol¬ 
low log. However, the origin of the 
canoe itself is of even greater contro¬ 
versy. The North American Indians 
had been experts in this mode of travel 
long before the arrival of the white man, 
and the canoe had been known in 
Europe for many* centuries before Col¬ 
umbus discovered America. Indeed, the 
canoe, like the wheel, seems to have 
developed independently in many coun¬ 
tries the world over wherever pioneer 
man desired a means of travelling across 
water. The evolution of the canoe 
came, probably, from the crude dugouts 
of the Stone Age. There are four types 
of early canoes native to Canada: the 
cedar dugouts or pirogues or long 
canoes; the elm-bark canoes; the birch- 
bark canoes; the kayaks or oomiaks of 
the Arctic Eskimos. 

continued on next page 


’Toronto , Canada , February , 1957 


21 









Cedar dugouts, used by the Indians 
for hunting, warfare and trading, were 
made by shaping and then hollowing 
out by burning or digging the inside of 
a tree trunk. Some dugouts of rough 
work were heavy, unstable and of little 
use in fast water, but adapted for 
swamps. Others of lighter wood and 
better workmanship, were large enough 
to carry groups of people, while others 
were carved and colored for ceremony 
and pagaentry. Dugouts were adapted 
for use in the fiords of the north Pacific 
coast by the Haida Indians. These 
people were trained from childhood so 
they could propel their craft quickly. 
Captain Cook observed dugouts sixty 
feet long, made from one log and carry¬ 
ing up to twenty men. Settlers used the 
log canoe for hunting and fishing as 
well as to carry passengers and freight. 
In isolated areas these primitive means 
of travel persist in everyday use because 
they are easily constructed from local 
materials. 

For more temporary purposes than 
are served by the clugout or birch canoe, 
the elm-bark boat was used by many 
Indian tribes. They were rudely con¬ 
structed out of an entire roll of the 
bark of the swamp elm. It was sewed 
at both ends with tamarack roots and 
the seams were gummed. Two thwarted 
canoes of this type were seen in the 
spring by Samuel Strickland near God¬ 
erich, laden with sugar, traps and game. 
They seldom lasted the season, but 


were used where speed of manufacture 
was important. Most people preferred 
the more practical birch canoe for its 
lightness and toughness. 

The birch canoe is reputed to have 
been invented by Nanabozho, the myth¬ 
ical forefather of the Algonquin family. 
According to the legend, he built his 
own first canoe on Manitoulin Island 
and passed on his invention to the 
Chippewas thousands of years ago. 
There is no doubt that the birch canoe 
is of Indian origin or that the explorers 
such as Champlain and the settlers 
quickly adopted the canoe as the 
method of inland water travel before 
the railway and the steamship. In the 
east, the Indian women made excellent 
canoes, while on the Pacific coast taboos 
prevented women from participating in 
this art. Cedar ribs were bent into bow 
shape and laid on a form. Sheets of 
wetted birch bark were sewn together 
and lashed to the guwhales and ribs, 
using tamarack roots. Then the whole 
was varnished over with a thick gum 
and the seams were secured with resin. 
This craft was 12 to 20 feet long, water¬ 
tight, light, swift, buoyant, fairly durable 
and easy to manage. 

There were three principal canoe¬ 
building centres; Three Rivers on the 
St. Lawrence, Cedar Lake and Nootka 



22 


Canadian Camping 







on Vancouver Island. There are many 
variations of the four types of native 
Canadian canoe. The adventurers or 
voyageurs sped along in their light 
“north” canoes, carrying furs for the 
North West Company. Their red 
paddles were as bright as their “chan¬ 
sons”. Through the arrangement of 
song, the French added to the charm of 
canoe travel and made it easier to 
recruit voyageurs for the brigades. 

Samuel Hearne described another 
type of Indian canoe which he saw in 
the north on his third trip. The “Atha¬ 
pascan” canoe was flat-bottomed, with 
straight sides. This one was sharp at 
each end, propelled by a single paddle 
and portaged easily. Another type was 
the West Coast Salish or “Chinook”, the 
most buoyant and graceful dugout in 
any part of the world. It is character¬ 
ized by its peculiar prow of animal form, 
by its length of thirty to fifty feet and 
its capacity of sixty to seventy people. 
They are propelled by paddles and sails. 
This would indicate that canoe sailing 
is neither a white man’s invention nor 
a modern sport. 

No greater tribute to the canoe as 
part of our Canadian heritage can be 
found than in its use as a theme by such 
poets as Bliss Carman, D. C. Scott, 
Marjorie Pickthall, Isabella Crawford, 
Charles Roberts, Archibald Lampman 
and others. Pauline Johnson, famous 
for her legends of the “Lost Lagoon”, 
catches the magic of the canoe in her 
poetry. The Song My Paddle Sings is 
often quoted and still familiar to-day: 

“August is laughing across the sky 
Laughing while paddle, canoe and I 
Drift, Drift 
Where the hills uplift 
On either side of the current swift”.

AMONG 

OURSELVES 

by John Latimer 
Director , Camp Kilcoo 

We are all aware of the tremendous 
strides that camping in Canada has 
made during the last half century, and 
most of us are even more amazed at the 
growth which has taken place in the 
last decade. Many names will be cher¬ 
ished in the ‘Hall of Fame’ of camping, 
but one in particular will be remem¬ 
bered as one of the small number of 
men and women who had so much to do 
with the early development of organ¬ 
ized camping throughout this country. 

Charles F. Plewman made his first 
invesment in the youth of Canada at 
Lake Couchiching in 1904. From that 
year until 1955, he continually added to 
this investment and has gained untold 
dividends from his efforts in moulding 
the great change which has taken place 
in the camping movement. 

Wilbur Howard, one of the many 
Canadians influenced by Charlie Plew¬ 
man, refers to him as a man with a 
dynamic personality and a keen interest 
in boys and young men as individuals. 
“He has the ability to stimulate them 
on to better things, and is possessed with 
the creative power to present with deep 



CHARLES F. PLEWMAN 


penetration the ideals and principles 
which have influenced the lives of thou¬ 
sands of Canadians with whom Charlie 
has been associated”. 

These characteristics were first felt in 
1911, when Charlie directed a small 
camp at Rosebank, near Pickering, On¬ 
tario. From 1913 to 1917, he witnessed, 
as director, the growth of Camp On Da 
Da Waks, at Golden Lake, and following 
this he travelled to Winnipeg and Camp 
Stephens on the Lake of the Woods. 
However, in 1921 he returned to Onta¬ 
rio and assumed the post of Secretary of 
the Ontario Boys Work Board, a posi¬ 
tion he held until 1934. He recalls most 
vividly some thirty-five camps which he 
was instrumental in organizing, most 
particularly the training camp at Beau- 
soleil Island in Georgian Bay, where he 
will never forget the thrill he got from 
sharing with 125 volunteer workers who 
came from all parts of the province. 
When Charlie was being introduced to 
this group for the first time, the late 


24 


Canadian Camping 



Taylor Statten said, “Gentlemen, may I 
present your new leader, Charlie Plew- 
man ... a man with a tenacious spirit 
which drives him to fight even harder 
when the chips are down, and when the 
odds are against him . . .” Such short 
term camps as this at Beausoleil took 
him from Ottawa to Temagami, from 
Nippissing to the Grand River, and 
from Canoe Lake and Couchiching to 
his final camping site on Gull Lake in 
Haliburton. It was here in the height 
of the depression, and with Taylor Stat- 
ten’s words echoing in his ears, that he 
started Kilcoo Camp. 

During his travels however, one of 
Charlie’s most notable achievments was 
recognized, for he organized and drew 
up the constitution for what was the 
first of the present day Older Boys’ Par¬ 
liament. 

Charles Plewman has been connected 
with the Ontario Camping Association 
since its inception. In the beginning, 
informal meetings were held with other 
pioneers of the private camps. Such 
stalwarts as Cochrane, Statten, Chap¬ 
man, Miss Edgar, Miss Hamilton, and 
Miss Halliday shared together their 
experiences and worked as a team to 
further the aims of the camping move¬ 
ment throughout the country. 

With the advent of World War Two, 
Leopold McCauley instigated a move to 
have Charlie take over as Secretary of 
the Toronto Red Cross, and he held this 
arduous post until 1949. During this 
time, however, in 1945, Charlie was 
asked, as one of the younger members of 
the ‘Old Guard’ to accept the position 
of President of the O.C.A. It was his 
responsibility to bridge the gap between 
the old and new generation of camping 
enthusiasts . . . for many of the 

younger members were just returning 
from active duty overseas. It is safe 
to assume that during his term of office, 
the Ontario Camping Association took 


on its present form. Permanent quarters 
were needed, and these were found by 
Charles. The budget needed to be 
increased, for the financial situation of 
the O.C.A. offered little scope for the 
committee to further the needs of organ¬ 
ized camping. Charlie obtaned the first 
annual grant from the Ontario Govern¬ 
ment. A greatly increased budget was 
adopted and the first full time secretary 
was appointed. Working together with 
the secretary he sent a stencilled news 
bulletin to the members of the associa¬ 
tion, and the forerunner of the present 
periodical was published. 

Throughout his many years in the 
camping field, Charles Plewman has 
always been a guiding inspiration to the 
younger leaders now operating their 
own camps. The thousands of young 
men who have been in contact with him 
cannot help but share the enthusiasm 
and the sincere interest which he shows 
to them as individuals. Although I have 
only known Charles Plewman for twen¬ 
ty years, I have been able to glean from 
this close association, the characteristics 
which have made his life so happy and 
rewarding. I have always been deeply 
impressed with his ability to recognize 
the best in people, and his willingness 
to give them a second chance. I have 
often seen him objectively study the 
problems of a counsellor or staff’ mem¬ 
ber who was not following through on 
his duties or responsibilities. Charlie, 
realizing that personal problems may 
be affecting these young men, has taken 
considerable time in chatting with them, 
encouraging them to solve their own 
difficulties. His dynamic personality and 
understanding of human frailties has 
made them more aware of their obliga¬ 
tions to him and the camp, and as a 
result they go forward with a renewed 
interest in pursuing the finer details ol 
leading other youngsters. I have also 
been moved by his ability to move

Toronto , Canada , February , 1957

AN OPEN LETTER FROM . . 


THE BUDDY SYSTEM 

A reply to the open letter to the Red Cross, 
Water Safety Division,which appeared in our 
December 1956 issue of Canadian Camping. 


Of all the systems yet devised for the 
control of large or small groups of 
organized swimmers, the Buddy System 
has proved to be the most effective. 
There are bound to be problems in any 
kind of organization due to the number 
of variables involved. And so it is in 
organizing a waterfront at a camp. 
Numbers, facilities, time, etc.—all of 
these factors vary from one camp to 
the next. The Buddy System will 
always work, but it depends on you, the 
Waterfront Director. 

First and foremost, it should be made 
clear that any waterfront person who 
thinks that this thing, “the buddy sys¬ 
tem”, patrols the area, ensures safety 
and allows him to “rest back on his 
heels” had better enter some other field 
of endeavour. No job on any waterfront 
is easy. It demands intelligence, organi¬ 
zational ability, an over-dose of patience 
and good hard work on the part of each 
person involved. Here, we will attempt 
to answer the specific problems brought 
forth by our friend Mr. Smith, in the 
Decemer issue of Canadian Camping. 

1. We have never found that it takes 
any youngster much time to get 
going — especially if he is going 
swimming. He’ll get himself a buddy 
and nine times out of ten will be 
down at the waterfront entrance 
screaming for the staff to hurry 
things along. And the odd ones will 
be screaming just as lustily, for by 
this time most of them will have 
found themselves a partner from 
among the assembled mob. 


2. Neither are children completely irre¬ 
sponsible. Ninety percent will choose 
their bosom pal as their buddy. The 
remaining ten percent must be im¬ 
pressed with the responsibility of 
remembering their buddy. Even for 
little ones, this is not difficult and 
often takes the form of a game. 
Again effective initial training is 
important. 

3. The Buddy whistle may seem slightly 
annoying at first, but soon reactions 
become automatic and a whistle 
something to expect. Only the 
“squares” are caught more than a 
few feet from their buddies at the 
check. Your senior swimmers should 
certainly realize and respect the 
importance of such a safety measure. 

4. At the beginning of camp, the 
Buddy whistle must be blown quite 
frequently. But after effective train¬ 
ing, a check at ten-minute intervals 
is sufficient. You say that it is pos¬ 
sible for a person to drown in five 
minutes or less, and so it is. The 
Buddy System merely aids the nor¬ 
mal patrol system in preventing 
such a tragedy. 

5. There is no earthly reason for the 
checker to know each shivering body 
by name. His job is only to count the 
number of buddies. The check board 
or tag system is the basic method of 
control, identifying each swimmer 
by name. It is not necessarily based 
on the Buddy System. 


26 


Canadian Camping 


THE CANADIAN RED CROSS SOCIETY 


And now for an answer to Hank 

Smith’s biggest problem- how DO yon 

run a Buddy System? 

1. Orientation of your campers is most 
important. Before they lay eyes on 
the waterfront, the system should be 
explained clearly. 

2. Encourage the children to keep the 
same buddy for the duration of the 
camp period. It must be made clear 
that if, at any time, you have no 
buddy, YOU are rather special. You 
must come down to the waterfront 
and there you will be supplied with a 
partner tor that particular swim. It 
goes without saying that each swim¬ 
mer MUST remember his buddy. 

T There is ONE narrow entrance to 
the waterfront. Rope it off and 
make sure that everyone uses that 
entrance only. 

4. One staff member counts the swim¬ 
mers into the area by simply record¬ 
ing the number of buddies. Another 
staff member is necessary if a further 
check in the form of a check board, 
or tag system is to be used. Both of 
these may be non-swimmers. 

. r ). The Buddy whistle is blown by the 
ONE person in charge, who insists 
on complete quiet. Anyone who is 
not with his buddy, or who is not 
perfectly still within a few seconds, 
must be sent out. Send both of them 
—not just one. 

f>. At all times, buddies must swim 
with, and consequently watch, each 
other. This means constant indivi¬ 
dual supervision. If one swimmer 
rests, he sits watching his buddy 
swimming or diving close by. If one 
partner leaves, the other must report 
with him to the check-out point. 


There he is supplied with another 
buddy or joins another pair to form 
three. This group of three is broken 
up as soon as there is another buddy 
available. 

7. Patrolling a swimming area is one of 
the most boring jobs in this modern 
world, but it is also the basic safety 
measure in any programme. Your 
swimming area should be divided 
into sections for patrolling. A patrol 
never takes his eyes from his parti¬ 
cular section. He speaks to no one 
and no one speaks to him. When 
the whistle goes, he quickly counts 
the buddies in his section and reports 
the number to the person in charge. 
This person adds up all buddies and 
makes sure that this coincides with 
the number kept by the person who 
has checked in the swimmers. 

8. At the end of the swim, a Buddy 
whistle is blown, buddies counted, 
and immediately the “all out” signal 
is sounded. Make sure that the 
swimmers leave the waterfront 
quickly, are counted once more, and 
are checked out on the check system. 
Towels, shoes, sweaters, etc. must 
be left completely outside the area. 

9. Much of the necessary respect for 
the hazards of water will come from 
your example. Remember, when the 
staff' swims the rules are no different! 

You say they have no fun. It can all 
be fun. It depends on you, Hank Smith, 
Waterfront Director, and your staff. 
But always remember, no amount of 
fun experienced by any number of 
people will make up for one life lost. 

Water Safety Service; 

Ontario Division 

Canadian Red Cross Society

Ethics ... 

As They Affeet 

Camp Directors 

by John Hoyle, Director, Camp GavVenture 


We who are camp directors have 
many, and perhaps increasing, problems 
to consider. One is that we must in all 
and every sense act and maintain stand¬ 
ards in our dealings with each other, 
our staffs, and parents, on the very high¬ 
est level. True, camps may be run pri¬ 
marily as business ventures or primarily 
as service ventures, but in either and all 
cases, we who by choice or appointment 
are in charge of camps must constantly 
be checking ourselves to be sure that, in 
the words of Scripture, we “provide 
things honest in the sight of all men”. 

Whether we like it or not (and most 
of us don’t), there is keen competition 
for both staff members and campers. 
The writer knows from experience how 
very easy it is, with the pressures under 
which we live, to take some slight 
advantage which, when reviewed in 
the light of day, may not be absolutely 
above board. 

Camping is an ideal, it is a standard, 
it is the demonstration of living on 
the highest level. There is, therefore, 
thrust upon us a requirement that we 
cannot dodge, even if we wished to, 
of maintaining our ethical behaviour 
at a level utterly above any voice of 
criticism. 

It might help all of us to re-read 
very carefully the “Businesss Principles 
of the Ontario Camping Association”, 
which were adopted some years ago 
and which are still our daily guide. 


These Principles or “Code of Ethics” 
suggest certain areas to which each of 
us as Camp Directors should give our 
very careful attention. 

It is, perhaps, unnecessary to reiter¬ 
ate what is already in the Code directly 
or by inference, but it may help to 
clarify our thinking if we consider two 
or three of these: 

1. Directors need to have confidence 
in each other. There are many ways 
in which they can share any special 
ideas or achievements with others. 
There is no doubt that all will benefit 
more by co-operation than by competi¬ 
tion. 

2. Directors need to be very, very 
careful in their approach to staff and 
campers. Persons known to have been 
at another camp the previous year 
should never be approached. If an 
approach comes from a staff member, 
then the director of the previous camp 
should be communicated with before 
any negotiations for a new contract 
are made. 

3. Bidding up on honoraria is 
another cause of misery, trouble and 
heartache. The writer hopes the time 
may come when some common stand¬ 
ards for honoraria may be reached. 
This would be a difficult thing to do 
when conditions vary so much, but 
some such mutual arrangement would 
work wonders in smoothing out some 
of the hard feelings that have some- 


28 


Canadian Camping 


times arisen between directors. So, is 
it too much to hope that in this field 
as in others, we endeavour to practice 
that ideal standard, the Golden Rule? 

4. The scrupulous adherence to 
contracts, verbal or written, between 
Director and Staff, is another factor 
to which attention needs be given. 
(The writer is aware that a verbal 
contract is not worth the paper it is 
written on (!!) but the principle 
remains.) 

5. Questions of extras at camps are 
not always made sufficiently clear to 
parents, in advance, resulting in bad 
personal relations not only to the camp 
involved but to the whole camping 
movement. 

This article, which has been sub¬ 
mitted to several camp directors for 
approval before publishing, is presented 
in deep humility, with the knowledge 
that it is so easy for anyone to err, 
and in the hope that when difficulties 
do occur they be brought before a 
committee of the Association to be 
settled privately and without publicity. 
It is not written in the spirit of criticism, 
but only with the hope of assisting to 
maintain those grand principles which 
have made Canadian Camping some¬ 
thing of which Canadians are justly 
proud. 

Business Principles in the O. C. A. 

1. A director should actively affiliate 
himself with the professional organiza¬ 
tions in the Camping Field. 

2. Directors and counsellors should 
be willing to assist other directors and 
counsellors by giving such information 
and advice as they can impart without 
detriment to themselves or their work. 

3. It is unprofessional for a director 
knowingly to take the initiative in 
negotiating with anv counsellors, in¬ 


T or onto. Canada . February, 1957 


structors or employees, who, during 
the preceding summer, were associated 
with another camp, without consulting 
the director of the other camp, in the 
spirt of good will; or for the first 
director to carry on such negotiations 
after a counsellor has signed up else¬ 
where. 

It is also unprofessional for a director 
knowingly to take the initiative in 
negotiating with a prospective camper 
who, during the preceding season, was 
at another camp; or to carry on nego¬ 
tiations with a camper who has already 
been enrolled elsewhere. 

4. It is unprofessional for a director 
to enter, with the parent of a camper, 
into a secret or confidential agreement 
of such a nature as would result in the 
loss of the good will of the parents of 
the other campers, were the conditions 
of the agreement to become known. 
This provision is to be construed in 
order to prevent price cutting in direct 
competition with other camps, but not 
to prevent camps from giving bona 
fide scholarships. A scholarship is to 
be interpreted as being an honorarium 
granted by the camp director to a 
camper because of the inability of the 
parents to pay the customary fees. 

5. It is professional to use as refer¬ 
ences only those people who have 
reliable knowledge of the camp or the 
director, preferably both. 

6. It is unethical for a camp to 
advertise in its prospectus, any activ¬ 
ity or service for which it does not 
provide adequate leadership and facili¬ 
ties. 

7. If, in spite of the acceptance of 
this set of Business Principles, compli¬ 
cations should arise, members should 
report the matter to the Board, and 
refrain from discussing same outside 
the Association.

ONTARIO CAMPING ASSOCIATION 
MINIMUM STANDARDS FOR ORGANIZED 
CHILDREN’S CAMPS IN ONTARIO 


It has been recommended by the Board of the Ontario Camping Association that a set 
of Standards be mailed to every Camp Director twice each year. To emphasize the importance 
of these standards and to bring them to the attention of camping people across Canada, we 
are reprinting them, in Canadian Camping at this time. 


As adopted by the annual meeting of the Ontario Camping Association in 
1949, and amended by revisions on November 5, 1953, February 25, 1955, and 
April 12, 1956. These standards are not mandatory for membership in the 
Association, but it is expected that all camps holding a membership will maintain 
at least this standard of camping. 

• •'•"T «•’„ |\ 

Definitionr An organized children’s camp is one which accomodates more 
than twelve campers age five, to nineteen years, for more than 
one week. 

HEALTH AND SANITATION 

1. A camp must hold a license from, and satisfy the health and sanitation 
requirements of, the Ontario Department of Health, as per the Public Health 
Act, R.S.O. 137 C 299. 

2. (a) Drinking water supply must be approved by the Department of Health 

before camp opens. Where the sample tested indicates that chlorination 
is required, this must he operating satisfactorily before the opening of 
camp. 

(b) Where the water supply is from a protected well, or is chlorinated by an 
approved mechanical chlorinator, a sample of water must be tested by 
the Department of Health every two weeks throughout the season. Where 
the water is from any other source, it must be so tested weekly. 

(c) Where the camp uses a method for chlorination of any kind, the ortho- 
tolidin test must be carried out in the camp at least three times weekly 
to ensure the correct amount of residual chlorine. 

3. All milk must be pasteurized. 

4. Hot water bathing facilities or showers must be provided at least once a week 
when campers are in attendance for two weeks or more. 


30 


Canadian Camping 


5. (a) Every camp operating for more than two weeks and witli more than 30 
campers must have in residence throughout the season at least one of: 

(i) a graduate medical doctor licensed to practise in Ontario, 

(ii) a registered nurse. 

(b) Every other camp must have at least a mature staff member, experienced 
in first aid, or the St. John Ambulance Association Senior First Aid 
Certificate, or other equivalent qualifications. 

Every camp without a resident doctor must arrange, before*, the opening 
of camp, for a qualified medical doctor to be on call. 

Each camper must have a health examination by a doctor or public 
health nurse two weeks prior to going to camp. 

(b) Each staff member must have a similar health examination before the 
commencement of duties at camp. 

7. A mid-day rest period of not less than one hour must be provided for campers. 

8. Transportation shall be available at all times in case of emergency. If possible, 
the camp should have access to a telephone. 

9. The camp shall have suitable quarters where campers who are ill can be 
separated from the group. 

LEADERSHIP 

1. A camp shall have a program staff (exclusive of kitchen, maintenane and 
secretarial staff) on the basis of at least one such person to every eight campers. 

2. Each such program staff person shall be not less than 17 years of age. (This 
does not exclude the use of additional younger persons in junior staff 
capacities provided the camp meets the one to eight ratio required above.) 

3. In the absence of the camp director from camp, his authority must be 
delegated specifically to some other qualified mature person. 

4. No prospective staff member is to be engaged by a camp until the director 
contacts at least one person who knows the applicant. Where the applicant 
has been associated with another camp or children’s organization, the director 
must get a written or verbal report from this camp or organization as to the* 
applicant’s character and suitability for a camp position. 

5. In camps of more than two weeks’ duration, all staff members must have at 
least one half day per week entirely free from camp responsibility.

DUEL 


A regular feature in our 
magazine, edited by Miss 
Mary Barker, National Coun¬ 
cil, Y.W.C.A. 


A TUCK SHOP ... OF COURSE! 


Certainly we have a tuck shop at camp. It’s a headache; it involves extra 
time and book-keeping! (We operate on a banking system in which each camper is 
credited with so much money; no cash is used. Each camper has a card with the 
days of the week in columns along one side. The most popular items are listed 
down the second side, with several columns for ‘“sundries”.) But I consider it an 
essential which must be accepted as part and parcel of the day’s work. Honestly, I 
don’t see how we could do without it. When girls are isolated for a month or so from 
stores, there are necessities which they must have, from a toothbrush to replace 
the one dropped ‘somewhere’, or the soap which has gone down to feed the fishes, 
to stamps and stationary, not to mention the shampoo which is absolutely “it”. 
Candy tuck is a minor item, restricted to five cents a day; there are no biscuits, 
soft drinks, or potato chips available. 

Then there is the matter of films. The ardent camera fan loses so much if she 
cannot exhibit the finished picture to her friends. It is these same camera fiends 
who have to be watched or else they overstep their allowances so quickly. 

But outside of the need to be able to purchase a bathing cap to replace the 
split one, etc., there is a basic need to feel free to make the odd purchase. A camp 
should not try to cut all the ordinary experiences of every-day life; some familiar 
ones must he included. And there is the need to learn how to spend money and to 
keep within a set sum. Our juniors do not shoulder this reponsibility completely on 
their own, but they, too, are making a beginning. 

There seems to be even more to this shopping business. There are the mores 
which belong to the race, and apparently a woman shopping is one of them . . . 
even a very young woman. For they enjoy it so . . . the choosing, the chattering 
amongst the shoppers, the importance that they place upon it. I always chuckle 
when I see how our campers gather around the pump to gossip . . . with 
the occasional water fight on the side . . . and think of it as a habit which belongs 
to the ages. Shopping seems to belong in that same category. 

I don’t know what would happen to morale if we closed the tuck shop; in fact, 
I’d be afraid to risk it! 


32 


Canadian Camping 





ISSUES 


This month, the Issue about 
which our writers duel is: 
The Camp Tuck Shop vs. 
No Tuck Shop. 


NO TUCK SHOP FOR US! 


I think camps should not operate a Tuck Shop, as this particular feature of 
the program tends to emphasize the financial status of the individual camper. It 
is true most camps limit the amount of money the child may spend on food daily, 
hut it is not usual for any limit to be placed upon the amount which may he spent 
on other articles available in the tuck shop. 

It is natural for the campers to compare the amounts which they have for 
‘ tuck”, and the one who has two dollars to spend for a three-week period will feel 
inferior to those who have five, seven or even ten dollars to spend. Thus a 
barrier” is set up at the beginning of the camping period and it may be difficult to 
break it down—this means that one of the basic purposes of camp is being defeated. 

By providing a tuck shop, a problem arises of control of the food the children 
eat. The camp dietitian and cook plan nutritious, adequate and well-balanced 
meals for the campers. There should be no need, then, for these meals to be 
supplemented by candy and/or fruit which is sold, usually immediately following a 
meal. If additional food is to be given the campers, it would be much more 
satisfactory for it to be provided by the camp and at specific periods in the program. 
If the cost of such “extras” is not included in the camp fee, it may be possible 
for it to be payable to the camp authorities at the time of registration—a set 
amount per camper and then the extra food could be distributed at the discretion 
of the camp authorities and each child would be assured of her fair share. 

Such a system would also economize on staff and program time which is 
spent in the operation of the “tuck routine”, and would likewise abolish many 
severe headaches suffered bv the business manager in supplying the “tuck”. 


Toronto, Canada , February , 1957

WATERFRONT SAFETY 

1. All waterfront and watercraft activities shall be supervised by a mature person 
holding the Canadian Red Cross Water Safety Instructor’s Certificate, or the 
Senior Y.M.C.A. Lifesaving Certificate, or the Bronze Medallion of the Royal 
Life Saving Society, or equivalent qualifications, and with experience in water¬ 
front supervision. The term “waterfront director” shall apply to persons of at 
least 21 years of age. 

2. There must be an adequate life guard system whenever campers are in the 
water; that is, at least one life guard for every ten persons, free from all other 
duties during that period and giving his undivided attention to the safety of 
the campers. 

3. All watercraft equipment such as docks and diving boards, and all watercraft, 
must be inspected regularly and approved for safety; this to be the personal 
responsibility of the camp operator. 

4. The camp must have definite written and posted safety rules lor swimming 
and the use of watercraft, to apply to stafF and visitors as well as campers. 
Under no circumstances shall anyone swim alone. 

5. Individual swimming tests must be tried as soon after arrival at camp as 
possible, and before swimming is allowed other than in shallow water. 

6. Swimming and diving must he restricted to a marked, approved swimming 
area except in certain authorized swimming contests, in which a boat, manned 
by two persons and carrying adequate life-saving equipment, shall accompany 
each swimmer. 

7. All non-swimmers must he restricted to an approved enclosed shallow-water 
area. 

8. No person is to be allowed alone in any watercraft in water beyond his depth 
before he has passed the. camp test for that type of craf t. 

9. In camps where outtrips are conducted, swimming and watercraft regulations 
for outtrips must be clearly defined, posted and enforced. 

10. Watercraft, other than life-saving patrol boats, must not be allowed in an area 
being used for swimming; campers must not enter or cling to a patrol boat, 
except in an emergency. 

11. Precautions must be taken against overloading of watercrait.

An Orientation Course for 
Camp Counsellors 

Chairman — Mr. Lloyd W. Perry 

Members of The Ontario Camping Association have discussed the angles and 
possibilities of again sponsoring an Extension Course for camp counsellors, one that 
would cover eight to a dozen lectures, and would be completed before University 
students are deep in the throes of examinations. 

The dream is to come true this month, when the University of Toronto, 
Department of University Extension, will present “An Orientation Course for 
Camp Counsellors” commencing February 7th and ending March 28th, every 
Thursday evening from 7.30 p.m. to 9.30 p.m. 

It is hoped that any directors from anywhere in Canada who have staff 
members in Toronto will sponsor their attendance at this course which is to cost 
ten dollars for eight lectures. The programme is shown for the convenience of 
those who wish their staff to attend, and for those directors who can themselves be 
present. All will be given a very warm welcome.

continued from page 17 

This concern about human personal¬ 
ity means that every camper will be 
recognized as a unique individual. It 
has been said that nature never makes 
the same mistake twice—she made each 
one of us different. The camp program, 
therefore, will be tailored to fit, and all 
individuals will not be forced into a 
common pattern. 

In a camp where the highest devel¬ 
opment of human personality is put 
first, there is increased responsibility 
placed on the individual. Within sensible 
limits of health and safety, the camper 
is given opportunity for making deci¬ 
sions and choices. This is not done for 
him by rules and regulations imposed 
from above or rigid traditions and ob¬ 
servances imposed by past history. In the 
facing of personal problems, ready-made 
solutions are not handed to him but 
rather he is helped to help himself. 

While this putting of the highest 
development of the human personality 
first seems like a fairly obvious thing 
to do, it is not so easy as it seems. Like 
the fact that there is plenty of room at 
the rear of a crowded streetcar, it is 
sometimes easier seen by an outsider. 
Then, too, under pressure from immedi¬ 
ate things around you, it is not always 
possible to put into practice right away 
the course of action that you know to be 
best. In addition, we are living in a mod¬ 
ern world where human personality is 
often crushed by economic exploitation, 
poverty, greed, racial prejudice, wars. 

Nevertheless, difficulties to the con¬ 
trary, human personality is the most 
valuable thing there is. Dr. Arnold 
Gesell has been quoted as saying that 
the future of civilization depends upon 
the recognition of the dignity and worth 
of man. As camping people it is our 
privilege and challenge to work with 
human personality—“the strongest, most 
creative force now present in the world.”

With the camping season coming up, 
safety officers of the Ontario Depart¬ 
ment of Lands and Forests offer the 
following suggestions for accident-free 
water travel: 

Don’t overload boats or canoes. 
Know their carrying capacity and keep 
the heavy articles in the bottom. 

Make sure the cargo will not shift in 
waves from other boats or from wind. 
Load slightly stern-heavy. Carry extra 
paddles and painter rope or tump line, 
bailing pail, life preservers. 

Do not travel during heavy storms, 
or in strange waters after dark. 

Do not go near large animals swim¬ 
ming; they may try to climb in the 
boat or canoe.

THE WONDERFUL WORLD OF 
ARCHAEOLOGY 

Ronald Jessup 

The story of a grocer boy who was 
obsessed with finding the ancient city 
of Troy is told in THE WONDER¬ 
FUL WORLD OR ARCHAEOLOGY 
by Ronald Jessup which Garden City 
Children’s Books will publish this 
month. 

Heinrich Schliemann refused to be¬ 
lieve that the Homeric stories of Troy 
were simply pleasing legends and find¬ 
ing the City of Troy became his one 
great ambition. Since there was no 
money in the family to provide him 
with a classical education, the young 
German was first a grocer’s apprentice, 
then A cabin boy, and then a book¬ 
keeper to a firm in Amsterdam. While 
in Amsterdam, he mastered seven or 
eight foreign languages. His knowledge 
of Russian led to an appointment in 
St. Petersburg. Thenceforth his career 
was marked by one success after an¬ 
other until in 1868, after a period of 
archaeological study and world travel, 
Schliemann set out to search for Troy. 

He found a flat-topped mount which 
seemed to him to answer Homer’s de¬ 
scription of the city’s position and 
there, for several seasons, he and a 
hundred workmen dug down through 
nine successive decayed and buried 
cities. None of these cities had pre¬ 
viously been known to the men of the 
nineteenth century. 


His story is just one of many which 
tell how archaeologists are solving bit 
by bit the mystery of man’s history 
from evidence left by Cultures and 
peoples who have disappeared. Double¬ 
day & Company, Publishers, Toronto 
2. $3.49, 

THE SINGING WILDERNESS 

Sigurd F. Olson. 

Written by a University-Professor- 
Turncd-Guide who knows intimately 
the Quetico-Superior country, The 
Singing Wilderness explores with keen 
insight the permanent values of a be¬ 
loved, vast wilderness area. An ecolo¬ 
gist, Mr. Olson gives meaning to every 
tuft of moss, every rock crack; and he 
is able to explain not only variation in 
rock formations, but why they are so 
varied. The book is a living story of 
the outdoors we, as campers, know 
and love. He takes us through the 
seasons, writes of the ways of a 
canoe, the virtues of the pine knot, 
gives a story here and there of birds 
he has encountered, ski trails he has 
followed. This and more he writes 
about in an almost tender vein, for 
it is plain to be seen that he loves every 
inch of the way. Every word he puts 
down on paper is a dedication. Mc¬ 
Clelland and Stewart,* Limited, To¬ 
ronto. $4.50.

THE AQUALUNG TWINS FIND 
CHINESE TREASURE 

Frederick Falkner 

The author, a Canadian by birth, now 
lives in Vancouver and knows something 
of the ocean and its ways, having 
sailed to Alaska and the Panama. He 
places his story off the Pacific coast of 
America just south of the Canadian 
border and takes his heroes underwater 
for adventure, after they have received 
birthday gifts of long-desired aqua¬ 
lungs. 

“The details given of the skill and care 
required to use this apparatus will 
ensure that all readers can follow the 
story with knowledgeable appreciation. 
The twins are also blessed with reason¬ 
able and intelligent parents, and when 
one twin finds a small box on the sea 
bed, their father assists in opening it 
and having the enclosed Chinese manu¬ 
script translated by a Chinese friend in 
the city.” 

An excellent book for summer read¬ 
ing, the author has succeeded in writing 
the whole adventure in a rational and 
frank style which will appeal to the 
most sceptical teenager. J. M. Dent & 
Sons (Canada), Limited, Toronto 
$2.25. 

INDIAN SIGN LANGUAGE 

Robert Hofsinde 

Mr. Hofsinde and his wife have 
taught Indian Lore in summer camps, 
boys’ clubs and at camp counsellors’ 
training courses, their knowledge in this 
field having come from direct contact 
with the Chippewas, of which tribe Mr. 
Hofsinde was made a blood brother. 

“In this authentic handbook, with its 
concise text and more than two hundred 
illustrations, the author shows how to 
form the gestures representing over five 


42 


Canadian Camping 




hundred words in Indian sign language. 
The vocabulary ranges all the way from 
long-familiar words such as “tree” and 
“grass”, to modern ones such as “record- 
player” and “Technicolour”. 

“For present-day boys and girls, sign 
language is fun. But for Indian tribes 
speaking different languages, it was for 
many centuries the only means of com¬ 
munication. It was the language of the 
council ring, the buffalo hunt, the trad¬ 
ing post. Now, it can be fun for the 
camper or hiker, at camp, on overnights, 
during programme evenings”. George 
J. McLeod, Limited, Toronto. $3.00 

— • 

Tell It To Your 
Campers 

Why the fringe on the deerskin 
jacket? For the benefit of modern 
hunters, K. K. Irizawa, of the Ontario 
Department of Lands and Forests here, 
explains: “Early settlers found that 
when buckskins, general attire of most 
Indians, were exposed to rain, the fringe 
formed little rivulets which carried the 
rain away to drip off instead of soaking 
into the skin. The fringe also formed a 
sort of camouflage which concealed a 
definite outline of a man at a distance. 
Indian scouts, frontiersmen and hunters 
found this to be an extremely important 
feature. It also softened the rustle when 
passing through the brush. 

“They found, too, that deerskin would 
stop the wind which cut through normal 
fabrics and it didn’t catch on brambles, 
or rip and tear like fabric.” 

. . . from the Department of Lands 
and Forests: ‘It takes a minute to write 
a safety rule; an hour to hold a safety 
meeting; a week to plan a safety pro¬ 
gramme; a month to put it into oper¬ 
ation. It takes a year to win a safety 
award; a lifetime to make a safe 
worker or camper. But it takes only 
one second for an accident to destroy 
all the best laid plans of men ... It 
hurts to learn safety by accident!”

DIRECTORS' 

NEWS LETTER 


The camp director who has to cope 
with uneven or deep shorelines in his 
dock-building project can take heart at 
a new type of steel floating dock or raft ; 
this for use where extra deep shoreline^, 
fluctuating water levels, sharp drop- 
offs or muddy lake or river bottoms 
make leg-supported piers impractical. 
Designed for one-man installation, it 
replaces the old makeshift steel drum 
raft. It consists of the non-skid platform 
mounted on two sets of twin steel 
pontoons especially designed to provide 
load-carrying capacity in excess of 3,000 
lbs.—sufficient to carry 15 to 20 people, 
plus any necessary accessories. The 
basic unit begins at 6 feet wide by 16 
feet long—a size that has proved of 
greatest possible stability under most 
water conditions, riding the waves like 
a big boat. Any additional length and 
width can be achieved by adding regular 
6 foot by 8 foot floating sections. Water 
ballast can be added to the pontoons to 
bring the platform closer to the water, 
where desired, and special baffles are 
built into each pontoon for additional 
stability. 

The new floating dock can be used as 
a free-floating raft, anchored in deep 
water, or it can be part of an extended 


dock, shore-anchored by means of a 
special hinged approach section. This 
hinged section allows for free up-and- 
down movement, while still maintaining 
necessary side rigidity. In many instances 
the floating dock may be attached to 
a regular rigid pier to extend docking 
facilities into deeper water. 

A new heavy-duty boat lift has 
been designed to take care of the 
heavier and larger outboard motor boats 
—up to 800 lbs. It features heavier 
tubular steel construction and a larger 
capacity hydraulic lift mechanism that 
brings the boat out of the water in 
seconds, with minimum effort. 

The entire unit includes two walk¬ 
ways of steel, in non-skid pattern, with 
telescopic adjustable leg supports, boat 
cradle of double tubular steel reinforced 
construction, and a specially designed 
hydraulic hoist which lifts boat and 
cradle with a few easy strokes of a 
lever. It will handle any size and shape 
of boat up to 15 feet in length, and 
weighing up to 800 lbs. Easily mounted, 
it can be bolted quickly into position on 
docks or piers, in single or multiple 
units. It is designed for individual lake 
property owners, or in multiple units for 
municipalities, resorts, camps or group 
lake projects. Its sectional design affords 
easy handling, simple installation, quick 
and easy dismantling and storage.

It 9 s Your Conference! 


1957 holds significance for the Camp¬ 
ing Conference . . . we celebrate our 
tenth anniversary, ten years of bringing 
together camp directors and staff with 
North America’s top speakers in their 
field of work: Psychology, Group Work, 
Health and Safety,. Waterfront, Arts 
and Crafts, Public Relations, Child 
Management, Nature Lore and Nature 
Crafts, Maintenance and Management, 
Aquatics, Forestry, Conservation, Music, 
Standards, Staff Training . . . and 
that’s only a partial run-down. 

1957 holds significance, too, in that 
the Royal Yodc Hotel will again play 
host to our guests and a list of distin¬ 
guished speakers. Dr. Taylor Statten 
needs no introduction. His appearance 


on our programme points only to valu¬ 
able discussions and a wealth of infor¬ 
mation to create in us a broader under¬ 
standing of children and their needs. 

Anyone who has heard Mrs. Alice 
Turnham speak looks forward to the 
next opportunity to hear her. Director 
of the Redpath Museum, McGill Uni¬ 
versity, she has a love of the outdoors 
and all that grows or moves in it; and, 
added to that, she has the gift of being 
able to translate the meaning of that 
life to her listeners. Besides conducting 
sessions during the Conference, she will 
be our speaker at the closing banquet 
at the Royal York.

continued from page 25 

forward with the times, and with the 
camping movement. 

He was ever mindful of his duty to 
his campers and staff, and was most 
willing to listen to new ideas and plans, 
despite the fact that his mature mind 
might have presented some doubts, His 
staff were encouraged to present new 
policies and suggestions, and when pos¬ 
sible he strongly supported them. 

Though he is free from the responsi¬ 
bility of owning and directing a camp, 
he is by no means inactive. The summer 
finds him and his wife working in their 
summer home, darting about Gull Lake 
in his new outboard, or entertaining 
friends, their children and three grand¬ 
children. Charlie is doing some painting 
as well. The winter finds him curling, 
active in Rotary and serving on various 
community activities. 

I recall most vividly the final flag¬ 
lowering at camp in 1955. As the 
Kilcoo banner was being lowered from 
the yard-arm, Charlie turned to me and 
whispered. “Well, John, I fear this is 
my swan song”, and as he slowly moved 
away I could see in his moist eyes the 
recollection of the hundreds of times 
that this same flag had been lowered to 
indicate the close of day, and of the 
thousands of young men who had gath¬ 
ered round that flag-pole, ever conscious 
of their great leader who had guided 
them through many days of happy 
camping. As Charles Plewman looks 
back over such an active career, knowing 
that he has been a part of so many 
early beginnings, I cannot help but 
share this joy, and I accept the chal¬ 
lenge from him as an inspiration to 
continue to practice and follow his high 
ideals and worthy principles, to the 
attainment of wholesome, laughter-filled 
days of camping in Canada.

NATURE 
CRAFT 
IN CAMP 


Have you got prunes on the menu for 
camp this year? Probably! Well, when 
you eat your prunes, save those stones 
inside them. They are potential “ears” 
for animals that you can easily make. 

Include some peanuts in their shells 
for camp canteen. Oh no—you musn’t 
eat them, not all of them, as there you 
have a menangerie of skunks, ducks, 
rabbits, dogs, caterpillars, etc. Take a 
look at the peanut and see what it 
suggests to you. If you have water¬ 
melons or musk melons, be sure to keep 
their seeds, for they also are precious 
ears, beaks, legs or tails to be attached 
to the peanuts. 

Date stones make legs on oak apple 
animals. 

A walnut shell, a small acorn and 
melon seeds make realistic turtles. A 
peach stone and a hazel nut and there 
you have a duck! Paint it in bright 
colours. 


When you go out on your hike, watch 
for pine cones, beech nuts, oak apples 
(remember they are a gall, not the fruit 
of the oak tree), acorns and their cups, 
hazel cups, maple seeds, a few small 
twigs for arms and legs. Beech twigs 
with next year’s bud on the end are very 
good—the end serves as a “hand” on the 
end of the “arm” when you make dolls. 

You’ll need a few feathers, so watch 
for those too. If you can’t find birds’ 
feathers, perhaps you’ll get some small 
hen’s feathers when you go to the farm 
for your eggs. 

Now you’ll need a sharp knife, a pair 
of scissors, a piercer to make holes, some 
straight pins, glue and paint to colour 
the finished articles. Here are a few 
suggestions—so now go ahead and let 
your imagination carry you away and 
think of some more. 

— • 


From the notebook of 

Mrs. A. H. Stoddard,

WOODFIRE 


AND 


Cardie- light 

When Miss Mary Edgar delved into her 
knapsack of Memory, she wrote these verses 
for her campers, and they appeared in her 
first hook> Woodfire and Candle-light. Since 
it is now out of print, we reprint them for 
camp directors who will want to clip them 
. . . and keep them . . . “to recall all 
those happy adventures and friendships of 
camp days” 


TRANS-CONTINENTAL FLIGHT 

No more an earth-bound mortal, I 
Have climbed the pathways of the sky; 
Have brushed the clouds with silver 
wings 

And matched the birds’ high 
wanderings. 

The mighty hills their heads bend low 
As over their proud peaks I go; 

I leap from cliff to precipice 
Above the canyon’s dim abyss. 

Now the Painted Desert’s spread 
With canopies of grey and red, 

Then patchwork fields of varied hue 
With here and there a lake of blue. 
On slender wings I seemed to poise 
Where far below like children’s toys 
Some tiny towns flashed into view, 
Then faded out as on I flew. 

By western seas I hailed the dawn, 
Through azure skies I drifted on 
Beyond the sunset’s fading light 
Into the mystery of the night. 

No more an earth-bound mortal, I 
Must ever keep the breadth of sky 
Within my heart, and strive to meet 
The challenge of the Infinte. 


DRIFTWOOD POWDER 

A handful of driftwood powder 
Tossed on the fire at night 
Creates a subtle enchantment 
With a blaze of blue-green light. 

The magic of glowing memory 
Kindled by the flames, 

Brings to mind the beauty 
Of dear forgotten names. 

As I watch the flickering wood-fire 
In the blue-ish light I see 
That strange ethereal blueness 
Of the Grotto of old Capri. 

Again I catch a vision . . . 

A temple in far Cathay, 

The Temple of Heaven, with blue-tiled 
roof, 

Blue as a summer’s Day. 

I see a Rajah’s palace 
With exotic gardens wide, 

Where peacocks spread their blue-green 
tails 

And strut in stately pride. 

You too have your store of memories . . . 
If you would unlock them some night, 
Toss a handful of powder on your fire 
And dream in the blue-green light. 


Toronto , Canada , February , 1957

Delegates can look forward to such 
outstanding discussion leaders as C. R. 
Blackstock, Mrs. J. Harry Ebbs, Barry 
Lowes, Kirk Wipper, David Palter, 
Mrs. Ralph Raymer, Miss Kathryn 
Anson, Dr. Elsie Palter, Harold

It was Mr. C. F. Plewman who said, 
as he handed us the copy for his 
editorial on this very subject: “I have 
been interested in noting how some 
camps really ‘cash in’ on our confer¬ 
ences. Their staffs are there as large as 
life and twice as natural. No major 
meeting, no important group is held but 
what some of their members are pres¬ 
ent. You run across them in the halls, 
looking at exhibits, browsing around 
book displays, lunching in the cafeteria 
and meeting together as groups. 

“You have to hand it to their direc¬ 
tors. They have a way of sparking and 
coaching their young hopefuls. They 
know a good thing when they see it.” 


A practical idea if ever there was 
one! Polyethelene ground sheets cost 
only 50c, inexpensive enough to be re¬ 
placed should they be lost, strayed or 
torn. Several camp directors keep a 
stock on hand, some to be sold in the 
Tuck Shop; but one director tells us he 
supplies them for trip emergencies. He 
examines each tripper’s equipment, 
and if there are not two ground sheets 
in each pack, he supplies the extra 
polyethelene sheet free. The camper 
returns the sheet to stores after the 
trip. They are light for packing and 
storing, and possess excellent wearing 
qualities.

Foiled 


Again! 

Time was when any reference to 
aluminum called up visions only of pots, 
pans and tea kettles, light-weight furni¬ 
ture, ladders and machinery parts. To 
see it become a vital part of canoe trip 
equipment sounds definitely out of 
place, and to say that that same alumi¬ 
num today threatens to do away with 
the above-mentioned pots and pans 
savours of a paradox rather than any¬ 
thing else. 

We are thinking in terms of alumi¬ 
num foil, of course, and there is every 
possibility that it may oust the frying 
pan, stew pot and “billy” from their 
former place of importance in the pack- 
sack. Ask any tripping counsellor or 
camper who has cooked with foil on a 
trip or overnight. The answer is always 
the same: “Give me foil every time! 
... no sticky pots to clean!” 

Trippers can see no end to the possi¬ 
bilities in foil cookery. Literally every 
meal can be prepared this way, since a 
minimum of skill and imagination will 
produce frying pans, a reasonable fac¬ 
simile of a saucepan, and even a char¬ 
coal burner. 

Some meals are commercially packed 
so that the entire course is sealed in one 
packet. All the outdoorsman has to do 
is build himself a good bed of hot coals 
and place the packet on it for twenty 
minutes to half-an-hour, according to 
instructions, turning it at about half¬ 
time. 

In several camps, the packaging is 
done in the kitchen or trip room, as 
part of the trip’s preparation. Any 
desired combination of meat and vege¬ 
tables can be used:

Chicken legs or breasts, potato slices,

If steak is on the menu, we might 
suggest that it be cooked individually 
according to taste for rare or well-done 
meat. Simply wrap the steak in foil and 
secure it so that it does not become 
unwrapped in the cooking process. 

Tea-bisk or any pre-mixed muffin 
mixture can be taken dry to the camp 
site, the necessary water added, and 
spoonsful of the batter placed in indi¬ 
vidual pieces of foil, the whole sealed 
and placed in the coals to cook. This 
takes about ten minutes. The foil for 
the batter should be large enough to 
allow for expansion. 

Try baking potatoes in foil with their 
skins on. Slice the potato in half when 
it is raw, insert a slice of butter, a piece

of cheese, and, if desired, a slice of 
onion. Bake all this together in one 
piece of foil, allowing about half-an- 
hour, or longer for a large potato. 

Apples baked in foil cannot be sur¬ 
passed. Take along the cinnamon and 
brown sugar to place in the centre with 
a dab of butter after they are baked. 
Warn campers that the apples are ex¬ 
tremely hot when they come from the 
foil; the danger of steam burns is very 
high if the foil package is not handled 
carefully. 

The pastry expert on any trip can try 
his hand at pies or turnovers; a foil pan 
is excellent for delicious popcorn; oat¬ 
meal or any uncooked cereal can be 
prepared in the usual way in the foil 
container; bacon and eggs or French 
Toast can be fried with ease. 

To make a pan, find a forked-stick 
sapling, leaving the two prongs at least 
two feet long. Make an oval of the two 
prongs by wrapping them around each 
other. In this frame tuck double sheets 
of foil, wrapping them securely around 
the edges. 

A square pan can be made by securely 
folding a piece of foil at each of the four 
corners; this can be placed on a toasting- 
grill, and held over the fire. 

Tripping counsellors bemoan the fact 
that on so many cook-outs meals must, 
of necessity, be cooked in the community 
pan. By this method, campers can only 
watch rather than experience the tech¬ 
niques of outdoor cooking. With foil 
cooking, each camper can learn to make 
his own utensils, learn to cook, learn to 
time a meal. He goes home a wiser 
child and a happier one. 

— m 


56 


Canadian Camping 







continued from page 15 

I have known Camp Directors who 
have operated camps without partici¬ 
pating in the “movement”. Frankly I 
have never been able to understand it. 
Surely no man or woman is so good that 
he or she can afford to say “I have no 
need of thee” or worse still to say, in 
effect, “I will do nothing to help you”. 
All of us will do a much better job in 
our respective camps if we share with 
others and become a part of all that is 
happening. 

The Camp Movement is made up of 
splendid folk. If we are not intensely 
proud of it, we should be. It is the great 
reservoir into which we pour the best 
of our combined experiences. If we 
value camping and its reputation, we 
will cherish it. And, moreover by attend¬ 
ing the Conference, or should I say “our 
conference”, I become a part of it all, 
for here the Movement takes on flesh 
and bones and becomes articulate. 

— • 


continued from page 49 

Buildings, Toronto, with remittance 
attached, payable to the Ontario Pro¬ 
vincial Treasurer. 

The other one would grace a Lodge 
or Dining Room, a beautifully illu¬ 
strated and printed poem produced by 
the Department of Lands and Forests 
of * Nova Scotia. It’s about 20”x26”, 
illustrating Authur Gutterman’s three- 
verse poem “Blessing On The Woods”. 
Surrounding the poem are delightful 
sketches of denizens of the forest— 
moose, bear, deer, mink, fox, rabbits, 
ground-hogs, large birds, small birds. 
This interesting piece of art work is 
available for the writing. Address: The 
Nova Scotia Department of Lands and 
Forests, Halifax, N.S.
